utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm the GP. Tell me what happened with your back and how it's been since?
reply: It happened on Saturday when I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden and felt a twinge, then I woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been three days now. The pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock, and it gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair, but feels better lying still with a heat pack, though it is definitely worse by the evening. I have worked from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
Good news, Daniel. Your examination shows the nerves to your legs are working perfectly — strength, reflexes and feeling are all normal, and the nerve stretch tests don't bring on leg pain. The pain and spasm are in the muscles beside the spine on the left. This is a very common strain of the back, and most people are much better within a couple of weeks and recover fully within about six weeks.

About the MRI: I understand the worry, but a scan isn't recommended here. It wouldn't change the treatment, and scans in people without back pain often show "disc bulges" and wear that are completely normal and can cause needless worry or procedures. We scan when there are warning signs, and you have none.

Plan:
- Keep moving gently — walking short distances often, avoid long bed rest or lying on the couch all day. Change position every 20–30 minutes at the desk.
- Heat packs are fine.
- Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food for up to a week, and you can keep the paracetamol going regularly (1 g up to four times a day) alongside it. Stop the ibuprofen if you get stomach pain, black stools or reflux.
- I'll avoid strong opioid painkillers — they don't help much for this and you've reacted badly to tramadol.
- A physio can help with exercises if it's slow to settle.

Come back urgently or go to the emergency department straight away if you get numbness around your bottom or private area, trouble passing urine or holding your bladder or bowels, weakness or numbness in your legs, or fever. Otherwise see me in 1–2 weeks if it isn't improving, sooner if it's getting worse.
reply: Are you sure I shouldn't have an MRI? I have been really worried about a slipped disc and needing surgery, and I just want to know for sure what is going on in there.

utterance: It's a really fair question. Even if a disc were involved, the treatment would be exactly the same — staying active and pain relief — and surgery is only considered when there's a nerve problem like severe leg pain, weakness or bladder changes that don't settle, none of which you have. An MRI now could easily show things that are normal for a 41-year-old and lead you down a worrying path. If things don't improve over the next 4–6 weeks, or any of those warning signs appear, I'll reassess and we'll arrange a scan then. Does that sound reasonable?
reply: Okay, I suppose that makes sense since I figured I would need an MRI to see what is going on, but I will give this a try.
